summary: ML-KEM is a quantum-resistant KEM with three NIST parameter sets in FIPS 203. This document specifies how to use it in the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect encrypted content.

eli5.summary: This tells encrypted messages how to use a lock designed to resist quantum computers.

subtitle: How to use ML-KEM to protect encrypted email and other CMS messages against quantum computers.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax can carry KEM-based recipients, but there was no defined way to use ML-KEM there.
tldr.mechanism: ML-KEM is used directly in the KEMRecipientInfo structure from RFC 9629: the sender encapsulates a shared secret to the recipient's public key, derives a key-encryption key with HKDF, and uses it to wrap the content-encryption key.
tldr.outcome: Each of the three ML-KEM parameter sets gets mandatory-to-support HKDF and AES key wrap choices. Hybrid use is not addressed. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9936 is a Standards Track Proposed Standard published in March 2026, and it is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It builds on RFC 9629 and the certificate conventions in RFC 9935.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ML-KEM is an IND-CCA2-secure Key Encapsulation Mechanism standardized in FIPS 203 by the NIST post-quantum project. It is the final standardized version and is incompatible with the pre-standard versions often called Kyber.

RFC 9629 defines the KEMRecipientInfo structure so that KEM algorithms can be used with the CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data content types. This document specifies the direct use of ML-KEM in that structure with ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. It does not address or preclude using ML-KEM as part of a hybrid scheme.
sections.eli5: There is already a standard envelope for messages that can be opened with different kinds of locks. This RFC says how to use one new quantum-resistant lock in that envelope.

sections.title: ML-KEM and Its Three Functions
sections.content:
ML-KEM is a lattice-based KEM built on Module Learning with Errors. The three parameter sets were chosen to be at least as secure as a generic block cipher of 128, 192 or 256 bits. Like all KEMs it provides three functions:

  • KeyGen() produces a public encapsulation key (ek) and a private decapsulation key (dk). It can start from a 64-octet seed, as described in RFC 9935.
  • Encapsulate(ek) produces a ciphertext (c) to send to the recipient and a shared secret (ss) for the originator.
  • Decapsulate(dk, c) gives the recipient the same shared secret.

Internally, all security levels use SHA3-256, SHA3-512, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256.
sections.eli5: A KEM has three jobs: make a key pair, use the public half to make a locked box plus a secret, and use the private half to open the box and get the same secret.

sections.title: How ML-KEM Plugs into KEMRecipientInfo
sections.content:
ML-KEM MAY be used for one or more recipients of CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data or authenticated-enveloped-data. The recipient's RecipientInfo MUST be OtherRecipientInfo holding a KEMRecipientInfo. An originator MUST implement Encapsulate() and a recipient MUST implement Decapsulate().

The fields are filled in as follows:

  • version MUST be 0, and rid identifies the recipient's certificate or public key.
  • kem MUST be one of id-alg-ml-kem-512, id-alg-ml-kem-768 or id-alg-ml-kem-1024, and kemct is the ciphertext for this recipient.
  • kdf: implementations MUST support HKDF with SHA-256 (id-alg-hkdf-with-sha256), with the parameters field absent. Other KDFs MAY be supported.
  • kekLength is the key-encryption key size in octets. ukm is optional and the RFC puts no requirements on it.
  • wrap: ML-KEM-512 implementations MUST support AES-Wrap-128; ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 implementations MUST support AES-Wrap-256. Other algorithms MAY be supported.
sections.eli5: The envelope has labelled slots: which lock was used, the locked box, how to turn the shared secret into a wrapping key, and how the message key is wrapped. The RFC says what must go in each slot.

sections.title: Underlying Components and HKDF
sections.content:
The components used with ML-KEM in KEMRecipientInfo SHOULD match a minimum desired security level. If you use something other than the defaults above, the key derivation and key-encryption strengths must at least match the ML-KEM level: 128-bit for ML-KEM-512, 192-bit for ML-KEM-768 and 256-bit for ML-KEM-1024. For AES Key Wrap with ML-KEM-768 a 256-bit key is typically used because AES-192 is not as commonly deployed.

When HKDF is used with KEMRecipientInfo, the salt is unused, that is, the zero-length string. Implementations MUST confirm that the requested output length L is consistent with the key size of the key-encryption algorithm.
sections.eli5: The wrapping tools must be at least as strong as the lock. A strong lock with a weak wrapping string would be the weak link.

sections.title: Certificates and S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
ML-KEM needs a static recipient public key, which the originator gets from the recipient's X.509 certificate. How that key is carried in the certificate is defined in RFC 9935.

An S/MIME implementation MAY announce support for ML-KEM by putting one of the ML-KEM OIDs in the capabilityID field of an SMIMECapability in the SMIMECapabilities attribute. The parameters MUST NOT be present in that case.
sections.eli5: To send someone a locked message, you look up their lock on their ID card. Mail programs can also say which locks they understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9935 and RFC 9629 apply. Implementations MUST protect the ML-KEM private key, the key-encryption key, the content-encryption key, the message-authentication key and the content-authenticated-encryption key. All of those except the private key are ephemeral and MUST be wiped after use. Disclosing the private key could compromise all messages protected with it.

Key generation and encapsulation both rely on random numbers, and weak random number generators can leave little or no security. Implementations MUST NOT use intermediate values of encapsulation or decapsulation directly for any purpose, and SHOULD NOT reveal information about them through timing or other side channels.

Good practice is to use a given ML-KEM key pair in only one scheme. The RFC also points to formal validation such as the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program as a way to gain assurance an implementation is correct.
sections.eli5: Keep the main key very safe, wipe the temporary keys after use, use good random dice, and do not use the same key pair for several different jobs.
